📱 Put this on your phone's home screen
It opens full screen, with no browser bars.

Added to the home screen it behaves like a normal app — its own icon, its own window, and it launches straight into the dashboard. Your logged weights and measurements live on the phone itself, so they stay put.

iPhone and iPad
1. Open this page in Safari. It has to be Safari — Chrome on iOS cannot add to the home screen.
2. Tap the Share button, the square with an arrow coming out of it.
3. Scroll down the list and tap Add to Home Screen.
4. Name it and tap Add.
Android
1. Open this page in Chrome.
2. Tap the three dots menu, top right.
3. Tap Install app, or Add to Home screen if that is what yours says.
4. Confirm.
Getting the Claude icon instead of this one? That is expected if you added it from a shared Claude link. The page runs inside Claude's own page there, so your phone saves Claude's icon and never sees this one. Nothing is wrong with the app — it just needs the page to be the top-level page. Either of the two fixes below gets you the right icon.
Fix 1 — iPhone Shortcut with a custom icon
The trap: the Choose Icon option inside the Shortcuts editor only offers Apple's built-in symbols and colours. It will never show your own image. The custom picture can only be set on the Add to Home Screen sheet, at the moment you place it. That is the step people miss.

0. First save the icon image into Photos. Press and hold it wherever you have it, then Save Image. If it only landed in Files, that is fine too — you will pick Choose File instead of Choose Photo later.
1. Shortcuts app, tap +.
2. Add Action, search Open URLs, choose it, paste the app link into the field.
3. Tap the shortcut's name at the very top to open its menu.
4. Choose Add to Home Screen. Do not tap Choose Icon.
5. A preview appears with a small square icon to the left of the name box. Tap that square.
6. Pick Choose Photo (or Choose File), select the icon, then tap Add top right.

Already placed one with the wrong icon? You cannot change it in place. Press and hold it on the home screen, remove it, then run through the steps again from step 3. The shortcut itself can stay.
Fix 2 — host the page properly, for real app behaviour
Serving this file at its own address is the only way to get the whole thing: the right icon, no address bar, its own window in the app switcher, and a normal Add to Home Screen with no Shortcut in the way. All the metadata for that is already built into this file and takes effect the moment the page is served on its own.

GitHub Pages does this free from the repository this app already lives in. The catch on a free account is that the page is public, and your height, weight and age are written into the file. Ask me and I will move those into settings you enter on your own device first, so the published copy carries no personal details at all.

🎯 Bulk or cut? Start here
Don't bulk yet. Run a recomposition first.

You want more muscle but carry noticeable belly fat and don't feel athletic. Those two facts point the same way. A bulk adds calories on top of what you already store as fat, and the leaner you are when you start one, the more of that surplus goes to muscle instead of fat. Bulking from where you are now would make the belly your first complaint, not your last.

The good news is you do not have to choose. Training five days a week with protein around 2.2g per kg, you can add muscle while slowly losing fat. That is recomposition, and it is realistic for anyone who is not already a very advanced lifter. Your BMI of 25.2 is not the problem here — muscular people score high on BMI. Where the fat sits is the useful signal, which is what the waist check below is for.

cm
How to know it is working. Track waist and weight together, not weight alone. During a recomposition the scale can barely move for weeks while your waist shrinks and your lifts climb — that is exactly the result you want, and a scale-only view would tell you that you were failing. Aim to lose about 0.3-0.5kg per week; faster than that and you start giving back muscle.
This is fitness guidance, not medical advice. Waist thresholds are population screening tools, not a diagnosis. Abdominal fat specifically is the kind most linked to metabolic and cardiovascular risk, so if your waist is in the high band, or you have any concern about blood pressure, blood sugar or cholesterol, get checked by a doctor rather than treating it as purely an aesthetic problem.
📊 Macro Breakdown by Goal

🥗 Vegetarian Meal Plans

Complete daily nutrition plans tailored to your goals

🛒 What to buy, in general
Keep these in and any day of the rotation is cookable without a special trip.

The per-plan shopping list above gives you exact amounts. This is the standing list underneath it — the things worth always having, and the ones worth buying big.

Protein — every shop
Fat-free Greek yogurt or skyr, in the biggest tub sold · Eggs, a dozen, plus a carton of liquid egg whites · Quorn mince and Quorn pieces · Your mushroom protein block · Cottage cheese · Semi-skimmed milk · Beyond Steak when you see it

Those cover four fifths of your protein. Everything else is seasoning.
Carbs — buy big, lasts months
Oats (1kg) · Basmati and brown rice · Wholemeal pasta · Potatoes and sweet potatoes · Wholemeal bread and wraps · Granola — but a small bag now, since it is a 20g topping rather than the base

All own-brand. Oats are oats, and rice is rice.
Vegetables — go frozen
Frozen spinach, peas, edamame and mixed veg are the single best value in the shop: cheaper than fresh, frozen at harvest so the nutrition is at least as good, and nothing rots in the drawer because you cooked a different day than you planned.

Buy fresh only for what you eat raw or want texture from — salad, cucumber, tomatoes, peppers, mushrooms, onions. Plus tinned tomatoes and passata, which are permanently useful.
Cupboard — buy once, lasts ages
Olive oil · Chia, flaxseed, pumpkin seeds · Goji berries · Nutritional yeast — check the tub says fortified with B12 · Cocoa powder · Peanut butter and almonds · Tinned lentils, chickpeas and black beans · spices

Tinned pulses deserve a special mention: cheap, no cooking, protein and a lot of fibre.
Buy protein in the biggest pack you will get through. Yogurt is the clearest example — the small individual pots often cost two to three times as much per gram of protein as the large tub of exactly the same thing. The same goes for cheese, nuts and oats. This one habit takes more off your food bill than any amount of hunting for offers.
Cheapest protein per pound, roughly in order: eggs, milk, own-brand Greek yogurt, tinned pulses, oats, then tofu and Quorn in the middle, and Beyond and THIS at the expensive end. That ranking is worth knowing because it lines up almost exactly with the protein-per-calorie ranking — the products that are poor value nutritionally are also the ones costing you the most. Leaning on the top of that list is cheaper and leaner at once.
Do not fill the trolley with these. Beyond Mince, Quorn sausages and nuggets, breaded anything, and mass gainers. Buy one of them when you fancy it, not as a weekly staple. And buy whey online rather than in the supermarket, where the same powder carries a large markup for the convenience.
🥄 Should you change your breakfast?
Yes — one change. Keep every ingredient, but make the skyr the base and the granola a topping.

Nothing in your bowl is wrong. The seeds, goji, cocoa and nutritional yeast all earn their place and I would not touch them. The problem is which ingredient you are eating most of. Granola is the most calorie-dense thing in the bowl at around 458 kcal per 100g, the least filling per calorie, and the easiest to over-pour — a generous heap is easily 70g, which is 320 kcal you did not plan for. On a deficit that alone can erase a day's work.

The numbers backed this up: before the change, breakfast was the least protein-dense meal in every one of the four plans. So I flipped the ratio. Same calories, same protein, same carbs and fat — but a far bigger, more filling bowl, and no protein powder needed at all.

 BeforeAfterWhy
Granola35-70g base20g toppingMost calories, least fullness, easiest to over-pour
Skyr100-150g300-375gProtein and volume for almost no calories
Whey powder16-20gnoneProtein now comes from food instead
Almonds—5-25gReplaces the fat lost with the granola
Seeds, goji, yeast, cocoaunchangedFibre, omega-3, B12, polyphenols — all worth keeping
Calories and macrosidenticalThis costs you nothing on paper
What you actually gain. Two to three times the bowl for the same numbers, which matters a lot when you are eating at a deficit and hunger is what breaks plans. Yogurt with seeds is also slower to eat and more satiating than dry granola. And weighing 20g of topping is far more accurate than judging a poured base by eye, so the plan you follow is closer to the plan on the screen.
If you want to go further on hard cutting days, a savoury breakfast beats any sweet bowl for fullness per calorie — Quorn mince or tofu scrambled with eggs, spinach and tomatoes, around 480 kcal for 44g of protein. You already eat Quorn, so it is no extra shopping. Alternate it with the bowl rather than replacing it.
To be clear, this is optimisation, not a rescue. Your breakfast was not bad — it was better than most. If you would rather keep it exactly as it is, the swap line under Breakfast in each plan gives you your original version at the same calories and protein. You would still get where you are going.
🍃 Diet quality, not just macros

Your breakfast is genuinely good

The granola bowl is doing more for you than most bodybuilding breakfasts. Chia and flaxseed give you ALA omega-3 and a large amount of fibre, goji and cocoa bring polyphenols, and nutritional yeast is a useful B12 source, which matters on a vegetarian diet. Keep it.

The one weakness was protein. As you were eating it, the bowl came to about 23g, which is under half of what your first meal should deliver. The plans fix that by making skyr the base rather than the granola — see the breakfast card above for the before and after. Whichever version you go with, weigh the granola rather than eyeballing it.

Worth checking: not every nutritional yeast is fortified with B12. Look at your tub, and if it is unfortified you are relying on the supplement alone.

Go easy on the ultra-processed side

Since you care about health and not only macros, the honest note is that Beyond Meat products are ultra-processed and relatively high in saturated fat and salt. They are a convenient way to hit calories on a bulk, but they are not the food to build every day around. Quorn is the better daily option — leaner, higher in fibre and less calorie-dense.

That is what the whole-food swap under every meal is for. Each one is matched on calories and protein, so you can cook from lentils, tofu, tempeh, paneer or chickpeas on any given day without redoing the numbers. A reasonable pattern is products on busy days, whole foods when you have time to cook.

The rest takes care of itself if you follow the plans: they clear 30g+ of fibre a day, lead with wholegrains, and put vegetables in most meals. Aim for two litres of water and some fruit and veg colour variety on top.

💡 Rest Day Recommendations

Days 6-7: Active Recovery

  • Skillrow or Excite Synchro — 20-30 min steady, low intensity. Both are non-impact and move blood through the legs without adding leg fatigue.
  • Skillmill in unpowered walk mode — 20 min easy. Save the sled and sprint modes for days you are not lifting hard.
  • Excite Recline if your legs are wrecked from Day 3 or Day 5 — seated, fully unloaded.
  • Mobility and foam rolling for 15-20 minutes
  • Focus on sleep quality (7-9 hours)

Recovery Tips

  • Consume protein within 2 hours post-workout
  • Stay hydrated: 3-4 liters of water daily
  • Manage stress with meditation or deep breathing
  • Take a deload week every 4-6 weeks

🥬 Protein-Rich Vegetarian Foods

Your go-to reference for high-protein vegetarian foods

🎯 Which protein should you actually eat?
Judge every protein by one number: grams of protein per 100 kcal.

You need around 205g of protein a day on a 2,406 kcal budget. Where that protein comes from decides whether that is comfortable or impossible. Hitting 205g costs you 932 kcal if it comes from whey, about 1,460 kcal from Quorn, and 2,563 kcal from Beyond Mince — which is your entire day gone with nothing left for carbs, fat or vegetables. Same protein, wildly different cost.

Tier 1 — build meals on these
Egg whites (21) · 0% skyr and Greek yogurt (17) · Beyond Steak (16) · Quorn pieces and mince (14)

These four should supply most of your daily protein. All of them give you 100g of protein for under 700 kcal. Skyr and egg whites are also the cheapest per gram of protein you will find.
14-21 g per 100 kcal
Tier 2 — good, use freely
Tofu (12) · Your mushroom block (11.9) · Quorn chicken bites (11.5) · Cottage cheese (11) · Tempeh (10.6) · Whole eggs (8)

Solid choices that also bring things the tier above does not — the mushroom block carries iron and omega-3, tempeh and tofu bring fibre, whole eggs bring the yolk nutrients. Rotate them for variety.
8-12 g per 100 kcal
Tier 3 — enjoy, but do not count on them
Beyond Burger (8.5) · THIS mince (8) · Beyond Mince (7) · Paneer (7) · Quorn sausages (6.7) · Quorn nuggets (5.5) · cheese, nuts

These are foods you eat because you want to, not because they move your protein along. Treat them as a meal you enjoy two or three times a week, and never as the thing carrying a day's protein.
Under 9 g per 100 kcal
Spread it, do not stack it. Aim for roughly 35-45g of protein in each of your five meals rather than a small breakfast and an enormous dinner. Muscle protein synthesis responds to each dose separately, so five good doses beat two big ones. Your plans are already built this way.
One thing that matters on a vegetarian diet. Plant proteins are generally lower in leucine, the amino acid that actually triggers muscle growth, so a plant-heavy meal needs to be slightly larger to do the same job. Dairy and eggs do not have this problem, which is your advantage over a vegan — use them. Mycoprotein is the standout among the meat alternatives here: the research on Quorn shows it supports muscle building at least as well as milk protein when the dose is matched. Pairing pulses with grains, as your plans do, also rounds out the amino acid profile.
On powder. If you want one, whey isolate is the most efficient protein you can buy at 22g per 100 kcal, and you already tolerate dairy. But note your plans now hit 200g+ without any powder at breakfast, so treat it as a convenience for busy days rather than something you need. Food first, powder to fill gaps. Seitan is worth a mention too at 20g per 100 kcal, though it is low in lysine so it should not be your only source, and it is pure gluten.
🥩 Which product to reach for

You now have four ranges in rotation and they are not interchangeable. The number that decides it is protein per 100 kcal — sort the table by that column. Anything above 12 is a protein source; anything below 9 is really a calorie source that happens to contain protein.

Quorn — the lean workhorse
Pieces and mince run 13-14g protein per 100 kcal, near chicken breast territory. This is what carries your protein target on a cut without eating your calorie budget. Note the crispy nuggets are a different animal at 5.5 — breaded, and not a protein food.
Best on a cut
Your mushroom protein block — quietly the best buy
19g protein at 160 kcal (11.9 per 100 kcal), plus 6g fibre and 30% of your daily iron in 100g, and real omega-3 from the flax, chia and hemp. Broad bean and pea protein rather than soya. Nutritionally this beats every Beyond product you own and it is the one I would use most outside Quorn.
High proteinHigh fibreIron + omega-3
THIS Isn't Beef Mince — fatty, but fortified
At 216 kcal and 13.3g fat per 100g it is a bulking mince, roughly where Beyond Mince sits at 8g protein per 100 kcal. What sets it apart is fortification: 100g gives about 40% of your B12 and 35% of your iron, plus 8.3g fibre. Beyond adds neither. On a vegetarian diet that is worth something real, so if you are choosing between two fatty minces, choose this one.
Calorie denseB12 + iron
Beyond Meat — mostly bulking, one exception
Built to eat like beef, which means added coconut and rapeseed oil. Your Jalapeño burger is 188 kcal and 16g protein per 100g patty — 8.5 per 100 kcal — and the mince is worse at 7. Good for adding calories, poor for adding protein.

Beyond Steak is the exception at 25g protein per 155 kcal. At 16.1 per 100 kcal it is the most protein-dense product you own. Keep it year-round.
Watch the fat
Portion them properly. All of these are less protein-dense per 100g than whey or paneer, so 100g is a side rather than a protein source. Build meals around 150-200g.
Salt is the shared downside. Your labels read 0.75g per 100g for the Beyond burger, 0.95g for the THIS mince and 1.00g for the mushroom block. A 200g portion of the block is a third of the 6g daily guideline from one ingredient. That is not a reason to avoid them, but if you eat them most days, keep the salt light everywhere else and drink enough water.

💊 Supplement Guide

Essential supplements for vegetarian bodybuilders

🥛 Choosing a whey — what actually matters
Buy whey concentrate, not isolate. And check it is certified vegetarian.

Isolate is marketed as the upgrade, and on paper it is: about 23g protein per 100 kcal against 20g for concentrate, with less lactose and fat. But across one or two scoops a day that difference is roughly 40 kcal, while isolate typically costs 30 to 50 percent more. You eat skyr, milk and cheese daily, so lactose is clearly not a problem for you. Concentrate is the better buy, and the money saved is better spent on food.

Isolate is only worth it if you are genuinely lactose intolerant, or you are deep in a cut and fighting for the last 50 kcal. Skip hydrolysate entirely — it is pre-digested for faster absorption, which makes no measurable difference to muscle growth, and it costs more and tastes worse.

The catch nobody mentions to vegetarians. Whey is a by-product of cheesemaking, and cheese is often made with animal rennet, taken from the stomach lining of calves. Plenty of whey powder therefore is not vegetarian, and most labels never say either way. Look for an explicit vegetarian certification on the tub, or a brand that states it uses microbial or vegetable rennet. If the label is silent, email the company and ask — the ones using microbial rennet will tell you happily. This is worth five minutes before you commit to a 2kg tub.
How to compare two tubs properly. Ignore the price per kilo, which is what the marketing wants you to look at. Work out the cost per 100g of actual protein: take the price, divide by the tub weight in grams, multiply by 100, then divide by the protein-per-100g figure on the label and multiply by 100. A cheap tub that is only 65 percent protein loses to a dearer one at 80 percent. Aim for at least 75g protein per 100g of powder for a concentrate.
Buy unflavoured. It is cheaper, it has a shorter ingredient list, and you already add cocoa and cinnamon to your morning bowl — so you get chocolate whey without paying for flavouring, sweeteners and the marketing that comes with them. It also disappears into skyr, porridge and curries without making them taste of vanilla.
Things to walk away from. Proprietary blends that do not break down what is in them. Products listing added glycine, taurine or creatine high in the ingredients, which can inflate the measured protein figure without adding usable protein. And mass gainers, which are mostly maltodextrin sold at protein prices.
Dose and timing. 25 to 40g per serving is the useful range; more in one hit is not wasted but does little extra. Timing matters far less than the marketing suggests — total daily protein is what drives the result, so a shake whenever it fits your day is fine. And remember your plans already reach 205g without any powder at breakfast, so this is a convenience for busy days rather than something the plan depends on.
